title: Bailer shells and shell tools

names.gloss: bailer shell used in the old time for a billy
generic term for shell; nautilus shell; button
mussel, found in fresh and brackish water

identification.basis: The dictionary's warkal 'bailer shell used in the old time for a billy' names the big Melo volute that Roth (1901, 1904) and Anderson (1996) record as the Bloomfield boiling pot, canoe bailer and water carrier. Roth wrote the species as Melo diadema and Anderson as Melo umbilicatus; both are names for the northern baler shell.

summary: The **[warkal](word:warkal)** is the baler shell, the big *Melo* volute of the northern coast, and the dictionary says exactly what it was: 'used in the old time for a billy' [ref:hershberger1982]. Roth wrote that boiling 'is done in a bark-trough ... or more usually in a large *Melo* shell', and that 'from the evidence of one of the earliest pioneers (Messrs. Hislop), it is a certainty that the Bloomfield blacks practised boiling before any permanent European settlement ever took place there', while Cook had found no boiling vessel sixty miles away at the Endeavour River and there was 'no such thing as boiling on the Tully River' [ref:roth1901]. The same shell, chipped down into a basin, was the water carrier of the whole east coast north of Bowen, the bailer in the [canoe](entry:canoes), the haft of the Bloomfield [woomera](entry:spear-and-woomera), and a trade good that found its way 'to considerable distances inland' [ref:roth1904] [ref:roth1909] [ref:roth1910]. Around it stands the rest of the shell kit: the nautilus and baler-shell spoons (**[jurungurr](word:jurungurr)**) that were 'very personal' things, the freshwater [mussel](entry:mussels) (**[mukirr](word:mukirr)**) used whole as a scoop, scraper and cutter, and the sharp *Cyrena* valve that cut bark [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1904] [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: **[warkal](word:warkal)** 'bailer shell used in the old time for a billy'. **[milbar](word:milbar)** is 'generic term for shell; nautilus shell; button'. **[jurungurr](word:jurungurr)** 'spoon made in old time'. **[mukirr](word:mukirr)** 'mussel. Found in fresh and brackish water. There are many up the Daintree near Bairds, some up Granite Creek. Has to be cleaned from the black stuff that tastes like tobacco' [ref:hershberger1982]. Other shells: **[dakaldakal](word:dakaldakal)** 'trocus shell'; **[kajarrbi](word:kajarrbi)** 'clam shell, the giant clam'; **[munji](word:munji)** 'big clam shell'; **[marakal](word:marakal)** 'spider shell'; **[kunkun](word:kunkun)** 'periwinkle, flat shellfish with a smooth shell'; **[ngarrakaja](word:ngarrakaja)** an edible shellfish; **[jalan](word:jalan)** the sea urchin, 'with a shell like a porcupine with prickles'; **[dumbul](word:dumbul)** 'any hard covering such as bark of a tree, crust of bread, shell of turtle'; **[kadan](word:kadan)** 'shell of turtle'; **[yijirr](word:yijirr)** 'shell of egg; fish scales' [ref:hershberger1982]. Roth's Cape Bedford (Guugu Yimithirr) name for the shell-boiler was *dirkai*, 'Melo diadema = shell-boiler made from it', and the Unio mussel scoop *warboparka* [ref:roth1901] [ref:roth1904].

sections.heading: The shell and what was made of it
sections.body:
**The basin.** 'The large "Lamp" (*Megalatractus aruanus*) and "Melon" (*Melo diadema*) shell is often used as a water-carrier. The latter, on the whole eastern coast-line north of Bowen, has the ventral surface of the last whorl, the spire, and columella chipped away so as to form a basin. If the shell be fresh, this removal may be effected straight away by means of a sharp piece of hard stone, the line of fracture following the tapping: otherwise, and the same holds good for all shell-work, it is soaked continuously in water for some three or four days previous to being manipulated. The chipped edge may be subsequently ground down with a stone. At the Bloomfield and on the Batavia River the melon shell is also used on the fire for boiling purposes' [ref:roth1904]. Near Whitsunday Island enough of the belly is cut away to leave the columella as a handle; along the Gulf from the Batavia down to the Mitchell River the shell is pierced for a thumb-hole instead [ref:roth1904]. 'From the eastern sea-board it finds its way, by trade and barter, to considerable distances inland' [ref:roth1904].

**Boiling.** Roth's food bulletin: 'Boiling is done in a bark-trough (e.g., *Curcuma australasica* on the Bloomfield), or more usually in a large *Melo* shell. I have met with the process in the hinterland of Princess Charlotte Bay, and on the Pennefather, but certainly in the latter case not as applied to the cooking of food. From the evidence of one of the earliest pioneers (Messrs. Hislop), it is a certainty that the Bloomfield blacks practised boiling before any permanent European settlement ever took place there. On the other hand, Lieutenant Cook, in describing the Endeavour River natives, only 60 miles distant, says: "They do not appear to eat any animal food raw; but, having no vessel in which water can be boiled, they either broil it upon the coals or bake it in a hole by the help of hot stones." There is no such thing as boiling on the Tully River' [ref:roth1901]. Anderson's informants agreed: [bark troughs](entry:bark-troughs) 'sat directly on the fire', or red-hot rocks went into the water in them, but 'the most widespread method of boiling, though, was in the large *Melo umbilicatus* shell' [ref:anderson1996]. On the Batavia the outer bark of the gum tree was 'boiled with stingaree-fat in a Melon shell' to make the cement for woomera pegs and spear joints [ref:roth1904].

**Bailer and haft.** Every canoe carried a shell bailer: 'in case of leakage, a shell-bailer', and the Bloomfield canoes used 'bailer shells ... to keep excess water out' [ref:roth1910] [ref:anderson1996]. On the Bloomfield, Endeavour and Cape Bedford ironwood woomera, the handle was 'either haftless or else hafted with two pieces of *Melo* shell fixed on with bees-wax, or else with a thin lath bent on itself' [ref:roth1909].

**Spoons.** 'Oval pieces of nautilus and melon shell are often used on the east-coast for spoons: indeed, on the Bloomfield and at Cape Bedford it is difficult to decide whether these should not rather be classed primarily as ornaments, they being fixed sometimes with wax, sometimes by means of a drilled hole, to a string hanging round the neck' [ref:roth1904]. Anderson: 'Spoons were made from a variety of materials. The most valued ones were those made with the scoop of nautilus or melo shells. Unmodified mussel shells were used as more temporary spoons or scoops. These shells, especially *Geloina coaxans*, were also used as scrapers (to remove ashes from cooked meat, for instance), or as a cutter. Only live shells were used to make these implements as dead ones cracked unevenly when worked.' The nautilus spoons 'were also very personal' [ref:anderson1996].

**Cutters and drills.** 'The edge of the valve of the *Cyrena jukesii* may be used for cutting bark, etc., on both the Eastern and Gulf coasts'; it cut the bow of the bark canoe and split the woomera for its peg; a Donax, Cyrena or mussel valve 'may also be used as a scraper in its entirety'; a sharp chip of Cyrena fixed into a split pencil of wood made the Gulf shell-drill, and shell was pierced for necklaces with tooth and stone drills [ref:roth1904] [ref:roth1910]. Shell hooks are on the [hooks and lines](entry:hooks-and-lines) page.

**Trade.** Cape Bedford 'send out or export ... nautilus-shell ... pearlshell chest ornaments and melo-shells'; the Bloomfield people took in 'shell-ornaments'; and the Endeavour and Bloomfield people who travelled up the Laura with red ochre, white clay and grass-tree spears were paid in melo shell, nautilus-shell necklaces, stingray spears and nets [ref:roth1910].

sections.heading: Telling the shells apart
sections.body:
- **Baler (*Melo*)**: the big smooth egg-shaped volute, orange-brown, the only shell large enough for a pot; *warkal* [ref:roth1904] [ref:hershberger1982].
- **Trumpet or 'lamp' shell (*Megalatractus*)**: long-spired, also used as a carrier; cut for a thumb-hole on the Gulf [ref:roth1904].
- **Nautilus**: the chambered pearly shell, cut into spoons and necklace plates; *milbar* [ref:roth1904] [ref:hershberger1982].
- **Clams** (*munji*, *kajarrbi*): heavy and white; a chipped piece was a pigment saucer on Mornington Island [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:roth1904].
- **Mussels**, salt and fresh (*mukirr*; *Geloina*; the river *Velesunio*): the everyday scoop, scraper and cutter, used whole and alive [ref:anderson1996] [ref:ala-mussel] [ref:hershberger1982].
- ***Cyrena***: the thick estuary cockle whose edge cuts bark [ref:roth1904].
- **Trochus, spider shell, periwinkle, urchin**: food and ornament rather than tools [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body:
- **Middens** of mussel and cockle on the river banks and the coast are camp sites; leave them [ref:acha2003].
- **A baler basin far inland** is a trade shell, carried up the Laura or along the coast [ref:roth1904] [ref:roth1910].
- **The chipped and ground rim**, the soot of boiling, and the drilled hole or wax of a spoon-ornament are the marks of use [ref:roth1904].
- **Live mussels** show as slits in the sand of a pool; the dead shells on the bank 'cracked unevenly when worked' [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Where the shells are
sections.body:
The baler lives on the sand and mud flats of the reef coast; Roth's basin was 'on the whole eastern coast-line north of Bowen' [ref:roth1904]. The nautilus washes up on the beaches; the clams are on the reef; *Cyrena* and *Geloina* are mangrove and estuary cockles [ref:roth1904] [ref:anderson1996].

Inland, the shell is the freshwater [mussel](entry:mussels), the dictionary's *mukirr*, 'Found in fresh and brackish water' [ref:hershberger1982]. The sea shells reached inland only by trade [ref:roth1904]. See each place above.

sections.heading: The shell in the kitchen
sections.body: The baler is the one vessel that goes on the fire, which is why Bloomfield cooking had a boiling stage that the Endeavour River, in Cook's account, and the Tully did not [ref:roth1901]. Boiling was part of the long processing of [yams](entry:yam) and the [leached](entry:leaching) foods, and of rendering fat and cooking shellfish; by the 1970s 'empty metal flour drums were used for boiling the yams' in the same place in the sequence [ref:anderson1996]. The shell spoon served the paste; the mussel scraped the ash off the meat from the [earth oven](entry:earth-oven); the *Cyrena* cut the bark for the [trough](entry:bark-troughs) and the [canoe](entry:canoes) that carried the baler [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1904] [ref:roth1910].

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body: Shellfish were gathered on the reef at low tide and in the mangroves in the dry season, and the trade in melo shell ran with the other barter, which on the Bloomfield was busiest 'during the laying-season at King's Lake country, i.e., whenever there happened to be a sufficient supply of food to attract them' [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1910]. A fresh shell is worked at once; a dead one is soaked for three or four days first [ref:roth1904]. See [the year on country](entry:seasons).

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
- Boiling pot on the fire, the Bloomfield 'billy' [ref:roth1901] [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:anderson1996].
- Water carrier along the whole east coast [ref:roth1904].
- Canoe bailer [ref:roth1910] [ref:anderson1996].
- Woomera haft, two pieces fixed with beeswax [ref:roth1909].
- Spoons of nautilus and baler, worn as ornaments on a neck string [ref:roth1904] [ref:anderson1996].
- Mussel valves as scoops, ash-scrapers and cutters [ref:anderson1996].
- *Cyrena* valve for cutting bark and splitting the woomera; shell chip drills [ref:roth1904] [ref:roth1910].
- Boiling bark with stingray fat for cement (Batavia) [ref:roth1904].
- Trade: melo and nautilus from Cape Bedford; shell for ochre up the Laura [ref:roth1910].

sections.heading: Making a baler basin, and boiling in it
sections.body:
From Roth and Anderson [ref:roth1904] [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1901]:

1. **Take the shell alive** if you can; a dead shell must be soaked in water for three or four days or it cracks unevenly [ref:roth1904] [ref:anderson1996].
2. **Chip away the belly** of the last whorl, the spire and the central column with a sharp piece of hard stone, tapping so that 'the line of fracture follows the tapping', until a deep basin is left [ref:roth1904].
3. **Grind the chipped edge** smooth on a stone [ref:roth1904].
4. **For a carrier**, leave the column as a handle (Whitsunday) or pierce the belly for a thumb (Gulf) [ref:roth1904].
5. **To boil**, set the basin on the fire with water in it and cook as in a [bark trough](entry:bark-troughs); or drop in hot stones [ref:roth1904] [ref:anderson1996].
6. **A spoon**: an oval piece of nautilus or baler, drilled or waxed to a string so it hangs at the neck [ref:roth1904].
7. **A woomera haft**: two pieces of baler shell set on the handle end with beeswax [ref:roth1909].
8. **A mussel tool**: use the live valve as it is, for scooping, scraping ash from cooked meat, or cutting [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
- Only live shells for tools; dead ones crack when worked [ref:anderson1996].
- Shell dust and edges cut; work shell wet.
- Taking shellfish on the coast for traditional use is recognised in the Marine Park and under the *Fisheries Act 1994*, within its rules [ref:gbrmpa-tu] [ref:qld-fishact].
- Middens are cultural heritage; take live shells, not old ones [ref:acha2003].
- The dictionary warns that the mussel 'has to be cleaned from the black stuff that tastes like tobacco' [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: The dictionary's gloss, 'used in the old time for a billy', dates the baler pot: the flour drum and the billy took its job, and by the 1970s flour drums boiled the yams at Bloomfield [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:anderson1996]. Roth's Bloomfield shells are in the Australian Museum's Roth collection [ref:khan1993].

locations.summary: The baler is a sea shell and does not live on the Hann; the shell of the river is the freshwater [mussel](entry:mussels), which the Thaypan people still gather [ref:fca-thaypan]. Melo shell came to this country by trade: about 1900 Roth found it passing from the Koko-warra of the Normanby to the Koko-rarmul of the Morehead, and he met boiling 'in the hinterland of Princess Charlotte Bay' [ref:roth1910] [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: Shells here
sections.body: The Atlas of Living Australia holds one record of a *Velesunio* freshwater mussel (2000) and none of the *Melo* baler in a box of about 90 × 85 km around the middle Hann, Laura and western Rinyirru [ref:ala-hann-shells]. A Thaypan man told the Federal Court in 2023 what he gets on Thaypan country: 'We get wallaby, barramundi, freshwater fish and turtles and mussels' [ref:fca-thaypan].

sections.heading: Shells at work here
sections.body:
**Trade.** 'At Princess Charlotte Bay, the Koko-rarmul of the Morehead River give the Koko-warra (whose "country" extends along the course of the Normanby and Deighton Rivers) reed-spears, iron-scraps, European tomahawks, etc., getting in return melo shell, grass-reed-spears, nautilus-shell necklaces, stingaree spears and fishing-nets' [ref:roth1910]. The Endeavour and Bloomfield people who came up towards the Laura were paid in the same goods [ref:roth1910].

**Boiling.** Roth: 'I have met with the process in the hinterland of Princess Charlotte Bay' [ref:roth1901].

**A shell scraper.** On the Morehead and Musgrave rivers, the settled wild-arrowroot meal was 'scraped up with a shell' and cooked in the ashes [ref:roth1901]. See [yams](entry:yam).

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: The upper Hann is the Possum People's country and the middle and lower Hann are Thaypan country, determined in November 2023 with rights to hunt, fish and gather [ref:fca-possum] [ref:fca-thaypan]. Ask them before taking mussels from the river.

locations.summary: At [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) the sea shell came only by trade, up the Laura road, but the mussel is in the river [ref:roth1910] [ref:ala-mussel].

sections.heading: Shells here
sections.body: Inland, the shell is the freshwater mussel. The Australian Museum holds *Velesunio angasi* from the Mitchell River a few kilometres from the homestead, and the dictionary's *mukirr* is the same kind of animal in the Daintree creeks [ref:ala-mussel] [ref:hershberger1982]. A baler at Karma Waters came up the trade road from the coast [ref:roth1910].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: The mussels are still in the Mitchell, and a baler brought up from the coast would work exactly as it did [ref:ala-mussel] [ref:roth1904].
